# 5.X Limitations of the Research

Every research study has limitations, and being honest about them is an important part of the research process. This section describes the main limitations of this study, explains their likely impact on the findings, and identifies where future work could address them.

---

## 5.X.1 Synthetic Dataset Generated by a Language Model

The clean training dataset of 10,080 utterances was generated using the Claude API (Anthropic), an AI language model, rather than collected from real hotel guests. While LLM-generated synthetic data is an accepted method in NLU research when domain-specific annotated data is unavailable — Bujel et al. (2021) demonstrated that fine-tuning BERT on even 1,000 domain-specific examples can outperform general models — it has known limitations.

Synthetic utterances may not fully reflect the vocabulary, phrasing, grammatical errors, or accent-specific expressions that real hotel guests use when speaking. For example, a real guest might say "AC no good", "I want service tomorrow morning not now", or use a mixture of Sinhala/Tamil and English words that a language model would not naturally produce. This means the reported accuracy figures (98.07% for Model A on clean text, 99.06% for Model C on Vosk output) are measured within a controlled synthetic distribution and may be optimistic compared to real-world deployment conditions.

This is acknowledged as the most significant limitation of this research. Future work should collect real guest request transcripts from hotel front-desk logs or conduct a field study to evaluate and retrain the model on authentic utterances.

---

## 5.X.2 Vosk Transcriptions Were Generated from TTS Audio, Not Real Human Speech

The Vosk-transcribed dataset (10,080 utterances used to train Models B and C, and to construct the test set) was produced by a two-step pipeline: each clean utterance was first converted to audio using Google Text-to-Speech (gTTS), and then transcribed back to text using Vosk. This means the "STT noise" in the training and test data reflects the transcription errors Vosk makes on synthesised TTS speech, not on real human speech recorded in a hotel room environment.

Real human speech introduces additional variability that TTS does not capture: speaker accent variation, pronunciation differences, background noise (air conditioning, television, conversations in adjacent rooms), microphone quality differences, and natural disfluencies such as hesitations and false starts. The actual accuracy gap between clean-text NLU and real-speech-to-Vosk-to-NLU pipelines may therefore be larger than the 8.73 percentage points measured in this study, and the recovery achieved by noise-aware training (Model C) may differ in a real deployment.

Despite this, the TTS-to-Vosk approach provides a controlled and reproducible method for generating paired training data at scale, which is the core methodological contribution. The findings demonstrate the principle that noise-aware training improves NLU accuracy in an offline pipeline — the specific magnitude of the gap would need to be re-measured with real speech data.

---

## 5.X.3 Tokenizer Mismatch Between Research Evaluation and Android Deployment

MobileBERT uses a WordPiece tokenizer, where words are split into sub-word units (e.g., "housekeeping" → ["house", "##keeping"]). The Python evaluation pipeline (Steps 3 and 4) uses the correct HuggingFace MobileBERT tokenizer, which is why the reported accuracy of 99.06% is achieved.

However, the Android implementation in `NLUService.kt` uses a simplified word-level tokenizer that splits text by whitespace and looks up each whole word in a `vocab.json` file. This means that any word not in the vocabulary is replaced with the unknown token, and sub-word tokenization is not performed. As a result, the actual intent classification accuracy on the Android device will be lower than 99.06% — particularly for less common words and hotel-specific terminology that require sub-word decomposition.

This tokenizer mismatch was a practical trade-off made to avoid the complexity of implementing a full WordPiece tokenizer in Kotlin. The NLU pipeline includes a rule-based keyword matching layer (Tier 1) which handles the most common hotel service requests before the MobileBERT model is invoked, which partially compensates for this limitation. Implementing a proper WordPiece tokenizer on Android, or using TFLite's built-in tokenization support, would be the recommended fix in a production deployment.

---

## 5.X.4 Single STT Engine Evaluated

This research uses Vosk as the only offline STT engine. The core finding — that there is an accuracy gap between clean-text NLU and Vosk-pipeline NLU, and that noise-aware training closes this gap — is demonstrated specifically for Vosk transcription noise patterns.

Other offline STT engines such as Whisper (tiny variant) or CMU Sphinx would produce different transcription errors with different characteristics. The size of the accuracy gap and the degree to which noise-aware training recovers it would likely be different for other STT engines. The general principle (that NLU models should be trained on STT-transcribed data to perform well in a real pipeline) is expected to hold across STT engines, but this has not been empirically validated in this study.

Future work could replicate the three-model training and evaluation pipeline with Whisper tiny as the STT engine to test whether the findings generalise.

---

## 5.X.5 No Real Hotel Deployment or User Acceptance Testing

The complete system — Android app, backend server, and staff dashboard — was developed and tested on a physical Android device connected to a local network. However, the system has not been deployed in an actual hotel environment or evaluated with real hotel staff and guests.

A real deployment would involve factors that were not tested in this study: the acoustic conditions of hotel rooms, the behaviour of guests unfamiliar with voice assistants, the workflow integration with existing hotel management processes, staff training requirements, and system reliability over an extended period of operation. Without this field evaluation, the claims about operational efficiency improvements and guest experience benefits remain theoretical, supported by the literature rather than direct measurement.

User acceptance testing (UAT) with real hotel staff and simulated guest interactions is identified as the most important next step following this research.

---

## 5.X.6 English Language Only

The system currently supports English only. In the Sri Lankan hospitality context, some hotel staff and guests may communicate more naturally in Sinhala, Tamil, or a code-switched mix of languages. Vosk supports Sinhala as a separate model, and the NLU model could in principle be fine-tuned on Sinhala or multilingual data, but this was outside the scope of this research.

Supporting multiple languages, or developing a multilingual intent classifier, is identified as a direction for future work.

---

## 5.X.7 Summary of Limitations

| Limitation | Impact on Findings | Mitigation in This Study | Future Work |
|---|---|---|---|
| Synthetic dataset | Accuracy may be optimistic vs. real guest speech | Accepted practice when real data unavailable | Collect real hotel utterances for retraining |
| TTS-generated Vosk transcriptions | Gap magnitude may differ with real speech | Demonstrates principle of noise-aware training | Re-measure with real recorded speech |
| Tokenizer mismatch on Android | Android accuracy lower than reported 99.06% | Rule-based Tier 1 compensates for common cases | Implement WordPiece tokenizer in Kotlin |
| Single STT engine (Vosk only) | Findings may not generalise to other STT engines | Vosk is the most practical offline choice | Replicate with Whisper tiny |
| No real hotel deployment | Operational claims are theoretical | System tested on real device, architecture validated | Conduct field study in a Sri Lankan hotel |
| English only | Limited applicability for non-English speakers | Target user group communicates in English | Add Sinhala/Tamil support |
